question: An otherwise healthy 31-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a several-day history of sharp, central chest pain, which is constant and unrelated to exertion. The pain gets worse on lying down and decreases with sitting forward. He has smoked 10–15 cigarettes daily for the past 7 years. His blood pressure is 120/50 mm Hg, the pulse is 92/min, and the temperature is 37.1°C (98.7°F). On physical examination, a scratching sound is heard at end-expiration with the patient leaning forward. ECG is shown in the image. Serum troponin is mildly elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? ?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Sharp, central chest pain" -> "Pain worse lying down, better sitting forward" -> "Scratching sound at end-expiration" -> "Mildly elevated serum troponin" -> "Acute pericarditis" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Sharp, central chest pain" -> "Pain unrelated to exertion" -> "Scratching sound at end-expiration" -> "ECG changes" -> "Acute pericarditis" -> 90%
CHAIN: "Sharp, central chest pain" -> "Smoker" -> "Mildly elevated serum troponin" -> "ECG changes" -> "ST-elevation myocardial infarction" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Sharp, central chest pain" -> "Pain worse lying down, better sitting forward" -> "Scratching sound at end-expiration" -> "Acute pericarditis" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Sharp, central chest pain" -> "Pain unrelated to exertion" -> "Smoker" -> "Normal temperature" -> "Costochondritis" -> 60%
analysis: The patient's symptoms and clinical findings are highly suggestive of acute pericarditis. The sharp, central chest pain that worsens when lying down and improves when sitting forward is characteristic of pericarditis. The presence of a pericardial friction rub, described as a scratching sound, further supports this diagnosis. The mild elevation in serum troponin can occur in pericarditis due to inflammation of the epicardium. The ECG, although not visible here, typically shows diffuse ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression in acute pericarditis, which differentiates it from ST-elevation myocardial infarction. The other options, such as costochondritis, pneumothorax, and bacterial pneumonia, do not align well with the described symptoms and findings.
